'''Kenneth Alan Ribet''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|r|ɪ|b|ɪ|t}}; born June 28, 1948) is an American [[mathematician]] working in [[algebraic number theory]] and [[algebraic geometry]]. He is known for the [[Herbrand–Ribet theorem]] and [[Ribet's theorem]], which were key ingredients in the [[mathematical proof|proof]] of [[Fermat's Last Theorem]], as well as for his service as President of the [[American Mathematical Society]] from 2017 to 2019. He is currently a professor of mathematics at the [[University of California, Berkeley]].

==Early life and education ==
Kenneth Ribet was born in [[Brooklyn]], [[New York City|New York]] to parents David Ribet and Pearl Ribet, both Jewish, on June 28, 1948.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.jinfo.org/Mathematics_Comp.html|title=Jewish Mathematicians}}</ref> As a student at [[Far Rockaway High School]], Ribet was on a competitive mathematics team, but his first field of study was [[chemistry]].<ref>Chapey, Dr. Geraldine. [https://www.rockawave.com/articles/chatting-with-chapey-50/ "Chatting with Chapey: Weber and Ribet Honored"], ''The Wave'', October 21, 2005. Accessed September 28, 2018. "Speaking of successful professionals, Kenneth Ribet is a world renowned scholar.... He is a proud graduate of P.S. 114, J.H.S. 210 and Far Rockaway High School."</ref>

Ribet earned his [[bachelor's degree]] and [[master's degree]] from [[Brown University]] in 1969.<ref name="Nomination">{{cite journal |url=https://www.ams.org/notices/201508/rnoti-p931a.pdf |title=Nomination of Kenneth Ribet |last1=Gross |first1=Benedict |author-link1=Benedict Gross |last2=Mazur |first2=Barry |author-link2=Barry Mazur |journal=[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]] |date=September 2015 |volume=62 |issue=8 |pages=931–956}}</ref><ref name="IAS"/> In 1973, Ribet received his Ph.D. from [[Harvard University]] under the supervision of [[John Tate (mathematician)|John Tate]].<ref name="Nomination"/><ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=32910}}</ref><ref name="IAS"/>

==Career==
After receiving his doctoral degree, Ribet taught at [[Princeton University]] for three years before spending two years doing research in Paris.<ref name="Nomination"/> In 1978, Ribet joined the Department of Mathematics at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], where he served three separate terms as supervisor of the department's graduate program, supervisor of the department's undergraduate program, and supervisor of the department's development.<ref name="Nomination"/>

Ribet has served as an editor for several mathematics journals, a book series editor for the [[Cambridge University Press]], and a book series editor for [[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]].<ref name="Nomination"/> He also served on the United States National Committee for Mathematics, representing the United States at the [[International Mathematical Union]], and was the Chair of the Mathematics section of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]].<ref name="Nomination"/>

From February 1, 2017 to January 31, 2019, Ribet was [[American Mathematical Society#2001.E2.80.93present|President of the American Mathematical Society]].<ref name="amspresident"/>

==Research==
{{Further|Ribet's theorem}}

Ribet's contributions in [[number theory]] and algebraic geometry were described by [[Benedict Gross]] and [[Barry Mazur]] as being "key to our understanding of the connections between the theory of [[modular form]]s and the [[ℓ-adic representation]]s of the [[absolute Galois group]] of the field of [[rational number]]s."<ref name="Nomination"/>

Ribet is credited with paving the way towards [[Andrew Wiles]]'s proof of [[Fermat's Last Theorem]]. In 1986, Ribet proved that the ''[[epsilon conjecture]]'' formulated by [[Jean-Pierre Serre]] was true, and thereby proved that Fermat's Last Theorem would follow from the [[Taniyama–Shimura conjecture]]. Crucially it also followed that the full conjecture was not needed, but a special case, that of [[semistable elliptic curve]]s, sufficed.<ref name="ribet">{{cite journal|last=Ribet|first=Ken|author-link=Ken Ribet|title=On modular representations of Gal({{overline|'''Q'''}}/'''Q''') arising from modular forms|journal=Inventiones Mathematicae|volume=100|year=1990|issue=2|pages=431–476|doi=10.1007/BF01231195|mr=1047143|url=https://math.berkeley.edu/~ribet/Articles/invent_100.pdf|bibcode=1990InMat.100..431R|s2cid=120614740}}</ref> An earlier theorem of Ribet's, the [[Herbrand–Ribet theorem]], is the converse to [[Jacques Herbrand|Herbrand]]'s theorem on the divisibility properties of [[Bernoulli number]]s and is also related to Fermat's Last Theorem.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ribet |first=Ken |title=A modular construction of unramified p-extensions of <math>\mathbb{Q}</math>(&mu;<sub>p</sub>) |journal=[[Inventiones Mathematicae|Inv. Math.]] |volume=34 |issue=3 |year=1976 |pages=151–162 |doi=10.1007/bf01403065|s2cid=120199454 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Washington |first=Lawrence C. |title=Introduction to Cyclotomic Fields |edition=Second |location=New York |publisher=Springer-Verlag |year=1997 |isbn=0-387-94762-0 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mazur |first1=Barry |name-list-style=amp |last2=Wiles |first2=Andrew |title=Class Fields of Abelian Extension of <math>\mathbb{Q}</math> |journal=Inv. Math. |volume=76 |issue=2 |year=1984 |pages=179–330 |doi= 10.1007/bf01388599|bibcode=1984InMat..76..179M |s2cid=122576427 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book | first1=John | last1=Coates | author-link1=John Coates (mathematician) | first2=R. | last2=Sujatha | author-link2=Sujatha Ramdorai | title=Cyclotomic Fields and Zeta Values | series=Springer Monographs in Mathematics | publisher=[[Springer-Verlag]] | year=2006 | isbn=3-540-33068-2 | zbl=1100.11002 | pages=3–4 }}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
Ribet received the [[Fermat Prize]] in 1989 jointly with [[Abbas Bahri]].<ref name="amspresident"/><ref name="Nomination"/> He was elected to the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1997 and the National Academy of Sciences in 2000.<ref name="amspresident"/><ref name="Nomination"/><ref name="IAS"/> In 2012, he became a Fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref>[https://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society], retrieved 2013-07-07.</ref><ref name="amspresident">{{cite web |url=https://www.ams.org/about-us/presidents/64-ribet |title=AMS President #64 Kenneth A. Ribet (2017–2018) |publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]] |access-date=August 4, 2020}}</ref> In 2017, Ribet received the [[Brouwer Medal]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://euro-math-soc.eu/news/17/03/2/2017-brouwer-medal-kenneth-ribet |title=2017 Brouwer Medal to Kenneth Ribet |publisher=[[European Mathematical Society]] |date=2 March 2017 |access-date=August 4, 2020 |archive-date=30 December 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201230125902/https://euro-math-soc.eu/news/17/03/2/2017-brouwer-medal-kenneth-ribet |url-status=dead }}</ref> For 2025 Ribet was awarded the AMS [[Leroy P. Steele Prize]] for Seminal Contribution to Research.<ref>[http://www.ams.org/news?class_id=1&expand=1&type=news Leroy P. Steele Prize 2025 for Seminal Contribution to Research]</ref>

In 1988, Ribet was inducted as a vigneron d'honneur by the Jurade de [[Saint-Émilion AOC|Saint-Émilion]].<ref name="IAS"/> In 1998, Ribet received an honorary doctorate from Brown University.<ref name="IAS">{{cite web |url=https://www.ias.edu/scholars/kenneth-ribet |publisher=[[Institute for Advanced Study]] |title=Kenneth A. Ribet |date=9 December 2019 |access-date=August 4, 2020}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Ribet is married to statistician [[Lisa Goldberg]].<ref>{{cite journal |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/notices/201703/rnoti-p229.pdf |title=Interview with New AMS President Kenneth A. Ribet |journal=[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]] |date=March 2017 |volume=64 |issue=3 |pages=229–232|doi=10.1090/noti1488 |last1=Jackson |first1=Allyn |doi-access=free }}</ref>
